claim: Gesture production helps the gesturer's own comprehension (meta-analysis: production d = .91, 17 samples; overall gesture d = .61), and single studies show benefits for working memory load in explanation, memory, and problem solving (the latter only for people with low visual working memory); no pooled effect is available for memory, explanation or problem solving.
agent_test: Mirror in text: force the model to write an explicit externalised step (sketch, table) versus silent reasoning at equal tokens.
audit_note: The .61 pooled d is Dargue's comprehension-only meta-analysis (gesture with speech, mostly observed); production alone is d=.91 on comprehension, and no pooled effect exists for memory, explanation or problem solving (single studies only, Pouw 2020 effect limited to low visual working memory).
claim_before_audit: Gesture production helps the gesturer's own cognition (comprehension, memory, explanation, problem solving), with a moderate to large pooled effect.

claim: Producing gestures beats merely observing them (d .91 vs .54).
agent_test: Compare model-written intermediate artifacts versus reading supplied ones at equal tokens.

claim: Gesture meta-analytic effect sits in comprehension of verbal information; it is not a direct test of thinking or problem solving, and heterogeneity is high (I2 69%).
agent_test: Do not cite d .61 as an effect on reasoning.

claim: Gesturing lightens working memory load during explanation, and meaningless movements do not.
agent_test: Dual-task proxy: add a memory-load side channel and compare agent with and without an external scratchpad.

claim: Preventing gesture changes strategy (more abstract rule use, fewer simulation strategies) but does not reliably lower accuracy. Encouraging gesture raised mental rotation and paper folding accuracy in one lab. Allowed vs prohibited did not differ in Chu and Kita Experiment 2. No preregistered replication found.
agent_test: Compare forcing the scaffold on versus leaving it optional, and removing it, on spatial puzzles at equal tokens. Expect a gain from forcing, little loss from removing.

claim: Co-thought gesturing speeds Tower of Hanoi 4-disc solutions without reducing steps (103.0 s non-gesturing vs 70.9 s spontaneous vs 80.1 s instructed) in Eielts et al. 2020 (not Pouw first author). Benefit only as an interaction with visual working memory, for roughly the bottom quarter to third of capacity. No spatial working memory interaction. Counts: 3-disc 27/11/35 (73), 4-disc 19/18/35 (72).
agent_test: Report scaffold gains by capacity and difficulty tier, not as a pooled mean.

claim: Gesture helps speakers find words (lexical retrieval hypothesis) failed a large conceptual replication: disfluency .07 prevented vs .06 allowed, p .30, 7,969 phrases.
agent_test: None needed; a caution against assuming gesture benefits transfer across tasks.

claim: Gesturing benefit depends on task type and learner: visuospatial learners gain on transfer, verbal learners do not (beta .43 vs .011).
agent_test: Stratify scaffold benefit by task spatial load.

claim: Gesture-speech mismatch is treated as a sign of readiness to learn (as reported in Wheeler's review of Broaders et al. 2007), and in Kersey et al. 2024 gesture-trained children retained math equivalence better at 4 weeks than action-trained children (.63 vs .42, Study 1); in Study 2 action-then-gesture beat gesture-then-action at 4 weeks (.57 vs .48), an advantage seen in non-mismatchers, not mismatchers.
agent_test: Not applicable to agent; background.
audit_note: The .57 vs .48 contrast is the order of training (action-then-gesture vs gesture-then-action, Study 2), not gesture retention vs other training, and in Kersey et al. mismatch status did not interact with condition in Study 1 and the order effect was in non-mismatchers; readiness-to-learn is only reported secondhand via Wheeler's review of Broaders et al.
claim_before_audit: Gesture-speech mismatch signals readiness to learn, and gesture training retains math learning at 4 weeks (action-then-gesture .57 vs .48).

claim: Gesture's cognitive role is consistent with conservative embedded cognition: aids thinking without being constitutively part of it; covert neural route cannot be excluded.
agent_test: Philosophical only; scaffold design needs no commitment.

claim: Gesture use follows cost-shifting: gestures rise with difficulty and fall with practice (Chu and Kita 2011: gesture rate fell across sections of the block, F(2,74)=6.12, p<.01). In LLMs, choosing when to externalise (adaptive grid switching reduced token cost on SpaRTUN; SwimBird mode switching improved several benchmarks) gives gains of varying size; no LLM study tests cost-shifting with practice.
agent_test: Test adaptive externalisation: allow the agent to choose when to write intermediate state and compare with always or never.
audit_note: d=.69 in Chu and Kita 2011 Exp 3 is the error-rate difference between gesture-encouraged and allowed groups, not the fall in gesture rate (Exp 2 gesture-rate decline: F(2,74)=6.12, p<.01, partial eta2=.14); also SwimBird gains over the base are not all small (e.g. WeMath 49.5 vs 38.8) and its token savings are not shown.
claim_before_audit: Gesture use follows cost-shifting: gestures rise with difficulty and fall with practice (Chu and Kita: gesture rate fell, d=.69). In LLMs, choosing when to externalise (adaptive grid switching, SwimBird mode switching) gives small gains and saves tokens in some cases; no LLM study tests cost-shifting with practice.

claim: Gesture and divergent creativity: adults show no clear mean gain from encouragement (Hyusein-Goksun style AUT fluency 6.09 vs 5.90 and 5.63) and a larger null (N=151, no group by trial effects); children gained fluency when encouraged (d=.98, N=54) but not originality or flexibility, and restriction did not significantly cut fluency. Habitual gesturing predicts scores.
agent_test: Do not expect externalisation to lift originality. If tested, count ideas and quality separately.

claim: In the searches run (12 gesture-specific LLM papers read, plus two more searches on finger counting and action simulation), no LLM study was found that tests whether gesture-like help improves the model's own reasoning; the nearest results were fine-grained action video benchmarks (CFG-Bench) and sensory norm tests.
agent_test: Gap, not testable directly.
audit_note: Universal negative ('No LLM study tests...') rests on the authors' own limited search, and the cited c24 url (arXiv 2401.17858) is a single-author project proposal on gesture understanding, not a synthesis supporting the 12/3/0 counts; CFG-Bench numbers (1,368 videos, 19,562 QA, 65.60/5.67 vs 95.85/9.05) do check out.
claim_before_audit: No LLM study tests whether gesture-like help improves the model's own reasoning in the gesture sense. 12 gesture-specific LLM papers were read earlier. Two more searches for finger counting and action-simulation tests found only fine-grained action video benchmarks (CFG-Bench) and sensory norm tests.

claim: Multimodal LLMs are poor at binding speech to pointing: human 96.9% vs Gemini-3-Pro 17.0%, rising to 42.9% with timestamped frames and verified ASR.
agent_test: Interface observability, not reasoning, is the bottleneck; supply structured inputs.

claim: LLMs recognise gestures weakly in free form (MIME 52.3% multiple choice, 19.8% free form; GestureGPT zero-shot top-1 44.79%).
agent_test: Background.
audit_note: Minor: MIME evaluates VLMs on mimed full-body actions, not hand-gesture LLMs; GestureGPT top-1 is on a function-mapping task.

claim: Models over-predict gesture meaning across cultures: recall 63-99% but specificity 1-61%.
agent_test: Background.

claim: Externalising spatial state as a grid or image improves LLM spatial reasoning on tasks where state is hard to track in text (VoT route planning 14.72 vs 9.48 CoT; Sketchpad +12.7% math, +8.6% vision; StepGame pruned grid gains of +13.5 to +42.0 points across six models). Gains are not at equal tokens: the grid route used 10x to 63x the text tokens. MentisOculi finds no gain from self-generated imagery over text.
agent_test: Compare text CoT, silent best-of-N text at matched cost and typed-grid redraw at equal total tokens.

claim: Externalised state fails in identifiable cases. VoT: state visualisation accuracy only 24-26% in navigation and tiling (the ring task is a separate small loss, GPT-4 CoT 52.5% vs VoT 49.5%, N=200, because it reduces to arithmetic). Self-drawn ASCII before answering fell below text-only in all base models; generated ASCII was correct only 12-50% of the time. Unified image models lose to text from compounding generation errors and cannot use even oracle images in some tasks.
agent_test: Verify the externalised state against the input before relying on it, and skip it when the task reduces to symbolic computation.

claim: LLM gesture generation works with explicit intent definitions: 43 of 49 speaker gestures fall in the rheme; 43.2% similar, 43.2% different but appropriate, 13.5% inappropriate.
agent_test: Background.

claim: Co-speech gesture as interface input speeds LLM interaction (43.65 s vs 91.11 gesture-only vs 108.58 voice-only, N=12).
agent_test: Not relevant to a text agent.

claim: Gesture founding dual-task result (Goldin-Meadow 2001): recall higher when gesturing, only on taxing lists. Children F(1,24)=11.32, adults F(1,31)=4.47; short lists n.s. Choosing vs being told not to gesture gave equal recall (9 children, 10 adults).
agent_test: Effect appears only under load: test scaffolds at high and low load.

claim: Grid or layout externalisation helps weaker and stronger LLMs, but the gain is not larger for weaker models (StepGame +13.5 for LLaMA3.1-8B, +25.6 Qwen3-8B, +42.0 LLaMA3.1-70B, +13.8 GPT-5.1). VoT also gained unreliably in weak models. Pouw-style low-capacity pattern is not mirrored cleanly.
agent_test: Report gains by model size and by construction accuracy of the grid, not just size.

claim: Adaptive choice of when to externalise helps a little and is learnable: switching on trust and complexity signals gave +0.4 to +1.6 accuracy on StepGame and -6.4% to -12.0% tokens vs grid-only on SpaRTUN, but +10.6% tokens for GPT-5.1 on StepGame; SwimBird learned text/visual mode choice and beat fixed baselines.
agent_test: Compare always, never and signal-triggered externalisation at matched total cost.

claim: Reasoning tokens alone did not help on visual puzzles: GPT-5.1 used about 13x more tokens under high reasoning with largely unchanged accuracy (MentisOculi). The equal-token advantage of externalisation over silent text reasoning has no clean test.
agent_test: Run the missing token-matched comparison.

claim: Training a model to construct a layout from text improves later text-only spatial reasoning (Qwen3-30B: StepGame +9.9, bAbI19 +17.0, SpartQA +43.3), unlike comprehension-only training (StepGame -6.1). This is fine-tuning, not a prompt-only scaffold.
agent_test: Not for the scaffold. Note only.

claim: Gesture-prohibition effect on accuracy has no preregistered replication. Alibali 2011 found equal accuracy (.91 vs .91; 89% vs 86%) with a strategy effect (parity .74 vs .91, p=.04); Chu and Kita found no allowed vs prohibited difference; Wassenburg 2018 failed to find the interference effect.
agent_test: Treat claims that preventing external tools harms accuracy as unsupported.
audit_note: Absence of any preregistered replication cannot be verified from the sources; Wassenburg 2018 addresses the gesture-induced interference effect, not gesture prohibition accuracy; all quoted numbers match.

claim: Source label correction: the Tower of Hanoi study cited as Pouw et al. 2020 is Eielts, Pouw, Ouwehand, van Gog, Zwaan, Paas (2020), Psychological Research 84:502-513. Count mismatch resolved (4-disc N=72, stated by the authors).
agent_test: Housekeeping.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-20 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors
